headline: Guwahati institute develops antivenom for two North-East pit vipers; use in patients awaits clinical testing
standfirst: The antivenom has so far been tested only in the laboratory and in preclinical studies. The standard Indian product is made against four other snakes.

body.text: Researchers led by the Institute of Advanced Study in Science and Technology (IASST), Guwahati, have developed an antivenom aimed at two pit vipers found in the North-Eastern states, the Ministry of Science and Technology said on 25 November. It is not available for patients: the ministry said further clinical and regulatory testing will be needed before it can be used routinely.

The two snakes are Pope's pit viper (Trimeresurus popeiorum) and the red-tailed bamboo pit viper (Trimeresurus erythrurus). The venom used in the work was collected in Mizoram and Meghalaya. The product is a bivalent antivenom, meaning it is made against two venoms, and is produced from horse antibodies.

In laboratory and preclinical studies it protected better against the venom of these two vipers than the Indian polyvalent antivenom did, the ministry said. It also reduced the blood-clotting disturbance and tissue damage that pit viper bites cause. The release gives no figures for the difference. The study has been published in the International Journal of Biological Macromolecules.
Why the standard antivenom falls short

Antivenom sold in India is made against the "Big Four": Russell's viper, the spectacled cobra, the common krait and the saw-scaled viper. When the health ministry launched its national snakebite action plan in March 2024, it said these four snakes cause around 90% of snakebites in India and that the polyvalent antivenom is effective in 80% of cases.

The North-East is where that product fits least well. The science ministry said its effectiveness against several medically important snakes of the region has been shown to be limited, and that bites from the two pit vipers are a common medical emergency there.

The action plan aims to halve snakebite deaths by 2030 and lists the provision of antivenom at all health facilities among its steps. The health ministry put the toll at around 50,000 deaths a year from an estimated 30 to 40 lakh snakebites.

IASST is an autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology. The team was led by its director, Prof. Ashis K. Mukherjee, and worked with Premium Serums and Vaccines Pvt. Ltd., Pune; Amrita Research Center, Delhi-NCR; Mizoram University; and Aaranyak, Guwahati. The release gives no timetable for clinical trials and does not say who would manufacture the antivenom.

citations.label: First North-East India-Specific antivenom developed against neglected Pit Vipers species (25 November 2026)
Union Health Ministry launches National Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Snakebite Envenoming in India (12 March 2024)

contributionNote: Sets the new antivenom against the health ministry's March 2024 snakebite action plan (Big Four cause about 90% of bites; polyvalent antivenom effective in 80% of cases; deaths to be halved by 2030) and makes plain that it is preclinical. The journal paper itself could not be opened in this run, so the study is described only as the PIB release describes it.

headline: Drug regulator cancels Sanofi's import papers for two vaccine ingredients after the company surrenders them
standfirst: The order covers purified tetanus toxoid and whole-cell pertussis bulk. Sanofi remains responsible for the quality of products already in the market.

body.text: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cancelled the permissions under which Sanofi Healthcare India Private Limited could import two vaccine ingredients, after the company surrendered them. The order, from the regulator's vaccine division, is dated 10 November and signed by the Drugs Controller General (India), Dr Rajeev Singh Raghuvanshi. CDSCO lists it on its website under 11 November.

The two products are purified tetanus toxoid, described in the order as a drug substance, and a bivalent inactivated suspension of Bordetella pertussis, the whole-cell pertussis component, in bulk form. The order does not name any finished vaccine and gives no reason for the surrender.

items: The import permission for purified tetanus toxoid, granted on 16 April 2010.
The registration certificate dated 25 August 2014, which covered both products.
The import licence for the pertussis bulk, dated 17 October 2014.

body.text: The import permission for the pertussis bulk, dated 21 August 2012, is not part of this step. The order records that CDSCO had already cancelled it on 10 July 2024. The latest order therefore closes the remaining paperwork for that product and ends the tetanus toxoid permission as well.

The order identifies the company as formerly known as Shantha Biotechnics Limited, and says it surrendered the permission, certificate and licence through an application on SUGAM, the regulator's online portal.

The order declares the cancelled papers ineffective and non-operative, so the company can no longer import either ingredient under them. Copies have gone to CDSCO's west zone office in Mumbai and to all its port offices.

The order is not a recall and records no quality finding against either product. It states that Sanofi will be responsible for the quality of products that were manufactured and are already in the market, and asks the company to submit its regulatory compliance filings, including safety reports.

citations.label: Order, File No. X-11026/95/2019-BD: cancellation of import permission, registration certificate and import licence for purified tetanus toxoid and Bordetella pertussis bulk (10 November 2026)

contributionNote: Separates what this order cancels from the pertussis bulk import permission CDSCO had already cancelled on 10 July 2024, and spells out what continues to bind the company. The order is a scanned page read by eye; the first list item and the registration-certificate wording should be checked against it before publishing.
